frameworks.name: ACA Framework
frameworks.definition: A three-step warm-outreach conversation sequence: Acknowledge something true about the person, Compliment them on it, then Ask a question that ties to the compliment and transitions toward the service being sold.

frameworks.name: 10-Step First Customer Acquisition System
frameworks.definition: A staged process for getting first paying customers from zero: build contact lists from email/social/phone, pick a platform, personalize outreach, send at volume, warm via ACA, invite referrals, offer free service, restart the list, raise price incrementally, and maintain list warmth ongoing.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a person starting a new business already possesses a usable lead list of far more contacts than they realize, composed of three sources: all email contacts, all social-media followers who can be DM'd, and all phone contacts. Combining these three lists produces substantially more reachable prospects than the founder typically estimates.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: zero paid advertising budget
pre-revenue stage
personal network exists
bounded_by: Does not apply to founders who have never communicated digitally with anyone and have no phone contacts

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that personalizing each outreach message with one observable detail about the recipient (e.g., a recent life event visible on their profile) meaningfully distinguishes the message from templated blasts and improves response rates, because it signals to the recipient that the sender invested a few seconds in them specifically rather than automating a generic pitch.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: warm-outreach to existing contacts
personal or semi-personal relationship exists
claims.mechanism: Personalization signals genuine attention, which lowers the recipient's defensive posture against perceived spam and increases the probability of a reply.
bounded_by: Cold audiences with no prior relationship — personalization at scale is impractical

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that reaching out to 100 people every single day from the combined contact list is the correct volume target for first-customer acquisition, and that the act of sending the first message is disproportionately hard relative to the second, because the psychological barrier — not the mechanics — is the primary obstacle.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder is pre-revenue or early-stage
outreach is to existing contacts

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when using the ACA framework (Acknowledge, Compliment, Ask), the ask should be tied directly to the compliment just given — for example, complimenting someone on balancing work and two kids, then asking how they find time to eat right and work out — because the logical connection between the compliment and the question makes the transition feel natural rather than transactional.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: warm outreach to personal contacts
service solves a problem the recipient likely has
claims.mechanism: Tying the ask to the compliment creates conversational coherence; the recipient perceives the interest in their problem as genuine because it was preceded by demonstrated attention.
bounded_by: Cold-traffic paid advertising contexts where ACA conversation flow is impractical

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that during warm outreach to contacts, a founder should NOT directly solicit the contact to buy, but instead ask if the contact knows anyone who is looking for the result the service delivers. This framing converts a potentially awkward sales ask into a favor request among acquaintances, which is psychologically easier for both parties.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: outreach to personal contacts or social followers
founder is selling a service or program
claims.mechanism: Asking for a referral to a third party repositions the interaction from transactional solicitation to a social favor, reducing the contact's defensiveness and the founder's discomfort.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a new founder should offer their first clients free service — explicitly in exchange for three things: the client actually uses the service, gives feedback, and leaves a review if they think it deserves one — because the founder's skill level does not yet merit charging, and free access generates more practice reps and faster skill improvement than any alternative.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder has zero paying clients
founder is in their first business
claims.mechanism: Free service removes the monetary barrier to trial, increasing reps delivered; more reps compound skill faster than theoretical preparation; feedback from real clients surfaces the hidden costs that prevent non-buyers from saying yes.
bounded_by: Does not apply once a founder has demonstrated results and can command pricing

Warren Buffett counterexample: Ben Graham declined free help from Buffett because the training cost exceeded Buffett's output value at the time — free can still be too expensive if onboarding cost is high

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that if potential clients decline to work with a founder even when the offer is free, the reason reveals hidden costs (time, effort, skepticism, logistical friction) embedded in the service offering. Identifying and eliminating those hidden costs enables the founder to charge significantly more later than competitors who charge without addressing them.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: pre-revenue or early-stage founder
offering service at no monetary cost
claims.mechanism: Rejection of a free offer signals that the perceived total cost (time, effort, skepticism, risk) exceeds perceived value; diagnosing and removing those non-monetary costs creates a differentiated offer at full price.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi estimates that reaching out to 3,000 people with a free service offer will produce approximately five takers, which he treats as a reliable baseline for early-stage warm outreach conversion.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: outreach to existing personal contacts and social followers
offer is genuinely free with no monetary cost
outreach is personalized not templated

numbers.axis: free-offer conversion rate across personal contact list

bounded_by: Cold paid-traffic audiences — warm personal network baseline does not translate

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the signal to start charging for service is not a specific time threshold but the onset of spontaneous referrals from free clients — referrals indicate the service is good enough that satisfied clients recommend it without being asked, which is the market signal of charge-worthy quality.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder is in their first business
has completed free client engagements
claims.mechanism: Referrals signal that perceived value exceeds zero cost; if people recommend for free, the service clears the minimum quality threshold for monetary pricing.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi prescribes a graduated price increase sequence for transitioning from free to full-price: after free clients, charge 80% off (20% of full price) for the next five clients, then 60% off, then 40% off, then 20% off, then full price — and optionally continue raising above full price as skill and delivered value improve. Each tier of five clients before moving to the next bracket.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder is transitioning from free to paid service
client base is still in the personal-network / warm-referral pool

numbers.axis: discount percentage relative to full price across client acquisition cohorts

anchors.value: can charge 20-40% premium above original full price

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that filling all available client slots with free and discounted clients creates genuine scarcity — because the founder literally has no capacity — enabling ethical, conviction-backed premium pricing for the next buyer who approaches, because the constraint is real.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder has finite service capacity
slots are actually filled
claims.mechanism: Actual capacity exhaustion creates credible scarcity; prospects who perceive real constraint are more willing to pay premium to secure access, because the constraint is not manufactured.
bounded_by: Does not apply to productized or infinitely scalable digital offers where capacity is unlimited

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that free clients generate revenue in three distinct ways: they leave reviews that attract paid buyers, they refer friends and family who become paid clients, and they themselves may eventually convert to paying clients — making free client relationships long-term business assets, not charity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder has delivered genuine value to free clients
founder maintains ongoing relationship with free clients
bounded_by: Free clients who received poor service — they generate negative reviews and churn referrals away

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that once a founder has paying clients who are filling capacity, they can convert existing free clients to paying by framing it as: a paying client needs the slot, so the free client must match the new rate or release the slot — and if the free client declines, the founder asks for the promised review and parts warmly.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder has reached full capacity
free client has already received value and is in ongoing service
claims.mechanism: Framing conversion as a practical resource constraint (not a sales pitch) reduces the free client's sense of being pressured; the paying-client slot justification is factual and removes the founder's awkwardness.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a founder should continuously warm their full contact list — even contacts who did not respond to outreach — by checking in, providing value regularly, and posting testimonials and results. Over time, sufficiently warmed contacts who have seen consistent proof begin to solicit the founder instead of waiting to be asked, eliminating active outreach need.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: ongoing after initial outreach cycle is complete
founder has some results/testimonials to share
claims.mechanism: Regular value deposits build goodwill; public testimonials reduce perceived risk for observers; the combination shifts the conversion trigger from founder-initiated outreach to prospect-initiated inquiry.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that an engaged lead is categorically distinct from a raw lead: a lead is anyone the founder can contact; an engaged lead is someone who can be contacted AND has shown demonstrated interest in the specific service being offered. Only engaged leads merit the next step of offering a free engagement.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when delivering a one-line verbal pitch in a time-constrained context, the minimum viable format is: I help [type of customer] get [dream outcome] in [time period] without [effort/sacrifice they fear], and I guarantee [X]. This collapses the full pitch into a single sentence that covers avatar, outcome, timeline, objection pre-emption, and risk reversal.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: verbal or in-person brief pitch scenario
founder has defined their offer clearly

examples.text: Alex Hormozi cited a personal example of a founder who approached him and offered to create short-form videos for Hormozi's existing content — at no charge, doing all the work including sourcing material from Hormozi's existing online content and posting it. Hormozi agreed because the founder had removed all hidden costs: no time required from Hormozi, no coordination burden. The founder started making the videos and subsequently began accepting payment, because the zero-friction free offer had gotten the engagement that demonstrated value.

Alex Hormozi referenced the historical anecdote of Warren Buffett offering to work for free for Ben Graham (the legendary value investor). Graham declined, telling Buffett he was overpriced even at free — meaning Graham's training cost to bring Buffett up to productive speed would exceed what Buffett could contribute. Hormozi uses this to illustrate that free work is not always advantageous to the person receiving it, and that the free client in a founder's first engagements is often actually getting the better end of the deal since the founder needs reps more than compensation.

Alex Hormozi gave a concrete scripted example of the ACA framework applied to a weight-loss service: after learning a contact is a working mother with two children, the founder says, 'Wow, you have two kids — you must be a super mom. Working full time and having two kids... how do you have time to eat right and work out?' This transitions naturally into the service conversation because the question surfaces a pain point (difficulty maintaining fitness habits) that the service addresses, without ever directly pitching.

Alex Hormozi scripted the precise referral ask a founder should use when talking to a personal contact: 'By the way, do you know anybody who is [describe their struggles], looking to [dream outcome] in [time delay]? I'm taking on five case studies for free because that's all I can handle. I just want to get some testimonials for my service or product.' He also offered an alternative humorous follow-up if the contact says no: 'Haha, does anyone you hate come to mind?' — noting this often elicits honest referrals.

practices.text: Start outreach on the platform where you have the most contacts — if you have more Instagram followers than email contacts, start there; if you have more phone contacts, start there.

When personalizing an outreach message, spend 30 seconds looking at the person's profile to identify one observable fact (recent job change, new baby, recent move, movie they watched) and use that as the opening of your message.
Offer free service with three explicit terms: (1) the client actually uses the service, (2) they give you feedback, and (3) they leave a review if they think it deserves one.
When a free client is displaced by a paying client needing the slot, ask warmly for the review you requested at the start of the engagement, regardless of whether the free client converts to paid.
Do not take on more than five free clients at once as a first-time founder — you will not be able to deliver quality beyond that.
Restart outreach at the top of the list after going through all contacts once — some contacts who did not respond the first time will respond on the second pass.
